stem.value: Researchers investigate eight enzyme inhibitors with the same molecular core and different substituents, R. They compare how two substituent properties relate to inhibitory potency.

Potency is measured by IC₅₀, the concentration that reduces enzyme activity by 50% under the assay conditions. A lower IC₅₀ indicates greater potency. Two dimensionless substituent parameters are considered:
Hydrophobicity H: larger values indicate a more hydrophobic substituent.
Electronic parameter E: positive values indicate electron withdrawal from the core; negative values indicate electron donation.
Note: Assume that H and E affect IC₅₀ independently.
Researchers describe the relationship in Table 1 using the following quantitative structure–activity relationship (QSAR). The model fits these idealised data exactly:

Here a, b, c and d are constants, with b > 0; log₁₀ denotes a base-10 logarithm. IC₅₀ is expressed relative to 1 nM, as shown. Assume the model applies to new analogues within the H and E ranges in Table 1. It describes an empirical relationship, rather than establishing a molecular mechanism.

questions.prompt: Four new analogues each have E = +0.5. Using Table 1 and the note above, which value of H would give the lowest IC₅₀?

steps.heading: Step 1 — Find the effect of changing E
steps.body: Compare compounds C and F. Both have H = 1.0, so H is held constant. E increases from 0 to +0.5, while IC₅₀ falls from 40 to 20 nM. Therefore this change in E multiplies IC₅₀ by 20 ÷ 40 = ½.

steps.heading: Step 2 — Apply the halving to each H value
steps.body:
As established in Step 1, increasing E from 0 to +0.5 multiplies IC₅₀ by ½. For each H value, take the IC₅₀ at E = 0 from Table 1 and multiply it by ½:

| H | IC₅₀ at E = 0 (nM) | Multiplier for E = +0.5 | Predicted IC₅₀ (nM) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.5 | 80 | × ½ | 40 |
| 1.0 | 40 | × ½ | 20 |
| 1.5 | 80 | × ½ | 40 |
| 2.0 | 640 | × ½ | 320 |

H = 1.0 gives the lowest predicted IC₅₀, 20 nM. Therefore the answer is B.

steps.heading: Shortcut
steps.body: All four candidates have the same change in E, so all four starting IC₅₀ values are multiplied by ½. Their ranking stays the same. Choose the H with the lowest IC₅₀ in the E = 0 series: H = 1.0.

eliminations.reason: H = 0.5 and H = 1.5 both give 40 nM, compared with 20 nM at H = 1.0.
H = 2.0 gives 320 nM. Increasing hydrophobicity does not always increase potency.

questions.prompt: A new analogue X has H = 1.5 and an IC₅₀ of 20 nM. Using Table 1 and the note above, what is its electronic parameter E?

steps.heading: Step 1 — Choose a comparison with the same H
steps.body: Compound D has H = 1.5, E = 0 and an IC₅₀ of 80 nM. D and X have the same H, so compare their E values to explain the change in IC₅₀. X has one-quarter of the IC₅₀ of D: 20 ÷ 80 = ¼.

steps.heading: Step 2 — Connect back to Question 1
steps.body: As established in Question 1, increasing E by 0.5 halves IC₅₀. X has one-quarter of the reference IC₅₀, so it must have halved twice. Starting from E = 0, two increases of 0.5 give E = 0.5 × 2. Therefore E = +1.0, which is option C.

questions.prompt:
Three new inhibitors, J, K and L, have hydrophobicity values H = 0.0, 1.0 and 1.5, used once each. Their electronic parameters are E = −0.5, +0.5 and +1.0, also used once each.

Their measured IC₅₀ values satisfy both of the following relationships:

J has four times the IC₅₀ of K.

K has four times the IC₅₀ of L.

Using Table 1 and the note about independent effects, which assignment is consistent with both IC₅₀ relationships? Each pair below is written as (H, E).

The compounds, data and question are original teaching material. The idealised data are constructed to fit the stated model exactly; they are not measurements of real inhibitors.

steps.heading: Step 1 — Start with a blank table and fill the H equals 0 row
steps.body:
Build the possible IC₅₀ values one row at a time. All values are in nM. Include E = 0 as a reference column; it is not one of the E values available for J, K and L.

| H | E = −0.5 | E = 0 Reference | E = +0.5 | E = +1.0 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 |  |  |  |  |
| 1 |  |  |  |  |
| 1.5 |  |  |  |  |

For H = 0, Table 1 gives compound A: E = 0 and IC₅₀ = 640 nM. Enter that known reference first:

| H | E = −0.5 | E = 0 Reference | E = +0.5 | E = +1.0 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 |  | 640 |  |  |
| 1 |  |  |  |  |
| 1.5 |  |  |  |  |

Increasing E from 0 to +0.5 halves IC₅₀, so 640 ÷ 2 gives 320 nM. Increasing E by another 0.5 to +1.0 halves it again, so 320 ÷ 2 gives 160 nM. Going backwards from E = 0 to −0.5 reverses a halving: double 640 to obtain 1280 nM. The first row is now complete:

| H | E = −0.5 | E = 0 Reference | E = +0.5 | E = +1.0 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 1280 | 640 | 320 | 160 |
| 1 |  |  |  |  |
| 1.5 |  |  |  |  |

steps.heading: Step 2 — Fill the H equals 1 row
steps.body:
For H = 1, use compound C as the E = 0 reference: IC₅₀ = 40 nM. Increasing E to +0.5 halves 40 to 20 nM; increasing E to +1.0 halves 20 again to 10 nM. Decreasing E from 0 to −0.5 doubles 40 to 80 nM. Add these values while keeping the first row:

| H | E = −0.5 | E = 0 Reference | E = +0.5 | E = +1.0 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 1280 | 640 | 320 | 160 |
| 1 | 80 | 40 | 20 | 10 |
| 1.5 |  |  |  |  |

steps.heading: Step 3 — Fill the H equals 1.5 row
steps.body:
For H = 1.5, use compound D as the E = 0 reference: IC₅₀ = 80 nM. Increasing E to +0.5 halves 80 to 40 nM; increasing E to +1.0 halves 40 again to 20 nM. Decreasing E from 0 to −0.5 doubles 80 to 160 nM. The table is now complete:

| H | E = −0.5 | E = 0 Reference | E = +0.5 | E = +1.0 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 1280 | 640 | 320 | 160 |
| 1 | 80 | 40 | 20 | 10 |
| 1.5 | 160 | 80 | 40 | 20 |

Now use only the E = −0.5, +0.5 and +1.0 columns. Select one entry from each H row and each of those three E columns; the E = 0 column was only used to build the table.

steps.heading: Step 4 — Use both IC50 ratios
steps.body: The two relationships require J : K : L = 16 : 4 : 1 in IC₅₀. J therefore has the largest IC₅₀, sixteen times that of L.

steps.heading: Step 5 — Test options A to D
steps.body:
Use the completed table to find J, K and L for each option. Both J ÷ K and K ÷ L must equal 4; satisfying only one relationship is not enough.

Option A Incorrect

J is (0.0, +1.0), giving 160 nM. K is (1.5, +0.5), giving 40 nM. L is (1.0, −0.5), giving 80 nM. Check the two ratios separately:

$$\,\text{J} ÷ K = 160 ÷ 40$$

$$\,\text{J} ÷ K = 4$$

$$\,\text{K} ÷ L = 40 ÷ 80$$

$$\,\text{K} ÷ L = 0.5$$

The first relationship holds, but the second fails: K has half the IC₅₀ of L, rather than four times it. Reject A.

Option B Correct

J is (0.0, +0.5), giving 320 nM. K is (1.0, −0.5), giving 80 nM. L is (1.5, +1.0), giving 20 nM.

$$\,\text{J} ÷ K = 320 ÷ 80$$

$$\,\text{J} ÷ K = 4$$

$$\,\text{K} ÷ L = 80 ÷ 20$$

$$\,\text{K} ÷ L = 4$$

Both relationships hold, and each H and E value is used once. B is correct.

Option C Incorrect

J is (1.5, −0.5), giving 160 nM. K is (0.0, +1.0), also giving 160 nM. L is (1.0, +0.5), giving 20 nM.

$$\,\text{J} ÷ K = 160 ÷ 160$$

$$\,\text{J} ÷ K = 1$$

$$\,\text{K} ÷ L = 160 ÷ 20$$

$$\,\text{K} ÷ L = 8$$

J and K have equal IC₅₀ values, and K has eight times the IC₅₀ of L. Neither required fourfold relationship holds. Reject C.

Option D Incorrect

J is (0.0, −0.5), giving 1280 nM. K is (1.5, +0.5), giving 40 nM. L is (1.0, +1.0), giving 10 nM.

$$\,\text{J} ÷ K = 1280 ÷ 40$$

$$\,\text{J} ÷ K = 32$$

$$\,\text{K} ÷ L = 40 ÷ 10$$

$$\,\text{K} ÷ L = 4$$

The second relationship holds, but the first fails: J has 32 times the IC₅₀ of K, rather than four times it. Reject D. Only B satisfies both relationships.

steps.heading: Shortcut
steps.body: Test J ÷ K first. The ratios for A, B, C and D are 4, 4, 1 and 32, eliminating C and D. Then test K ÷ L for A and B: the ratios are 0.5 and 4. Only B satisfies both conditions. A valid answer must satisfy both ratios and use each H and E once.

questions.prompt: Using the equation and Table 1, which expression gives the value of the coefficient c?

steps.heading: Step 1 — Substitute a compound that includes c
steps.body:
Choose compound G because H = 1 and E = 1 make the substitution simplest: H² is also 1, there are no 0.5 factors, and all four terms a, b, c and d remain in the expression. G has IC₅₀ = 10 nM, so:

$$log_{10}(\frac{1}{10}) = a - b + c + d$$

Use the logarithm rule to write the same relationship in exponential form:

$${log}_{A}(M) = N$$

is equivalent to:

$${A}^{N} = M$$

$$\frac{1}{10} = {10}^{a - b + c + d}$$

Since 1/10 = 10⁻¹, the exponent must be −1:

$$-1 = a - b + c + d$$

We want c, but a, b and d are unknown. We do not need to find them separately. Instead, look for another compound with the same H and E = 0: this keeps a − b + d unchanged and removes cE.

steps.heading: Step 2 — Finding a − b + d
steps.body:
To find a − b + d without the cE term, choose H = 1 and E = 0. H = 1 makes aH − bH² become a − b, while E = 0 removes cE. Compound C has these values and an IC₅₀ of 40 nM. Substituting into the equation gives:

$$log_{10}(\frac{1}{40}) = a - b + d$$

Recall the general logarithm rule:

$${log}_{A}(M) = N$$

is equivalent to:

$${A}^{N} = M$$

Here the base is 10, M = 1/40 and N = a − b + d. Applying the same rule gives:

$$\frac{1}{40} = {10}^{a - b + d}$$

steps.heading: Step 3 — Separate and replace the shared contribution
steps.body:
Compare the exponential forms from Steps 1 and 2:

$$\frac{1}{10} = {10}^{a - b + c + d}$$

$$\frac{1}{40} = {10}^{a - b + d}$$

Both contain the same a − b + d contribution. The exponent in the first equation also includes c. Using the exponent rule:

$${10}^{x + y} = {10}^{x} \times  {10}^{y}$$

Separate a − b + d from c in the first equation:

$$\frac{1}{10} = {10}^{a - b + d} \times  {10}^{c}$$

Step 2 tells us that 10ᵃ⁻ᵇ⁺ᵈ is 1/40. Substitute that known value:

$$\frac{1}{10} = \frac{1}{40} \times  {10}^{c}$$

Multiply both sides by 40:

$$\frac{40}{10} = {10}^{c}$$

$$4 = {10}^{c}$$

A base-10 logarithm tells us the power to which 10 must be raised. Since 10ᶜ = 4, c = log₁₀(4). No decimal logarithm calculation is needed.

steps.heading: Shortcut
steps.body: At the same H, C → G increases E by 1 and reduces IC₅₀ from 40 to 10 nM. The reciprocal quantity therefore increases fourfold. In the equation this corresponds to adding c, so 10ᶜ = 4 and c = log₁₀(4).

eliminations.reason: A and B give negative c values, which would make increasing E increase IC₅₀, contrary to C → G. C gives 10ᶜ = 2: this would predict 20 nM at E = 1, rather than G’s 10 nM. It confuses the factor for a 0.5 increase in E with the factor for a 1.0 increase.

questions.prompt: Let L = log₁₀(2). Which pair gives the values of a and b?

steps.heading: Step 1 — Choose compounds that remove cE and isolate d
steps.body:
We want a and b, so use compounds with E = 0: the cE term disappears. Compound A is especially useful because H = 0 also removes both aH and bH², leaving only d. Its IC₅₀ is 640 nM.

$$log_{10}(\frac{1}{640}) = d$$

Using the logarithm–exponential conversion rule from Question 4, write this as:

$$\frac{1}{640} = {10}^{d}$$

Next choose C and E. Their H values are 1 and 2, so substituting gives different combinations of a and b. All three compounds have E = 0:

| Compound | H | IC₅₀ (nM) | Resulting equation |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | 0 | 640 | $\frac{1}{640} = {10}^{d}$ |
| C | 1 | 40 | $\frac{1}{40} = {10}^{a - b + d}$ |
| E | 2 | 640 | $\frac{1}{640} = {10}^{2a - 4b + d}$ |

steps.heading: Step 2 — Make two equations containing only a and b
steps.body:
Compare A and E first. They have the same IC₅₀, so they have the same logarithm and therefore the same exponent:

$$2a - 4b + d = d$$

Subtract d, then divide by 2:

$$2a - 4b = 0$$

$$a - 2b = 0$$

Now compare A and C. C gives:

$$\frac{1}{40} = {10}^{a - b + d}$$

Separate out d and replace its factor using Step 1:

$$\frac{1}{40} = {10}^{a - b} \times  {10}^{d}$$

$$\frac{1}{40} = {10}^{a - b} \times  \frac{1}{640}$$

Multiply both sides by 640, then use the logarithm rule:

$$16 = {10}^{a - b}$$

$$a - b = log_{10}(16)$$

Since 16 is 2⁴, first write the logarithm as:

$$a - b = {log}_{10}({2}^{4})$$

The logarithm power rule states:

$${log}_{10}({x}^{n}) = n {log}_{10}(x)$$

Apply this rule with x = 2 and n = 4:

$$a - b = 4 {log}_{10}(2)$$

L was defined as log₁₀(2), so substitute L:

$$a - b = 4L$$

steps.heading: Step 3 — Solve the two linear simultaneous equations
steps.body:
Start with the first equation and rearrange it to express a in terms of b:

$$a - 2b = 0$$

$$a = 2b$$

Substitute a = 2b into a − b = 4L:

$$2b - b = 4L$$

$$b = 4L$$

Now use a = 2b again and substitute b = 4L:

$$a = 2 \times  4L$$

$$a = 8L$$

Therefore the answer is B.

steps.heading: Shortcut
steps.body: Equal IC₅₀ values at H = 0 and H = 2 require a = 2b, leaving B and D. The sixteenfold reciprocal change from A to C requires a − b = 4L. Only B satisfies both conditions.

eliminations.reason: A makes a − b zero, predicting equal IC₅₀ values for A and C. C makes a − b negative, predicting that C has a higher IC₅₀ than A. D satisfies a = 2b, but its a − b is 8L: it predicts a 256-fold reciprocal change, rather than the observed sixteenfold change.

questions.prompt: Researchers use a modified QSAR model:

contentBlocks.value: Here IC₅₀ is entered as its numerical value in nM. The coefficients a, b, c and d are constants, with c > 0. In this question, zero hydrophobic contribution refers to zero hydrophobicity.
For a series of compounds with zero hydrophobic contribution, which graph best represents how IC₅₀ changes as E increases?

steps.heading: Step 1 — Remove the hydrophobic contribution
steps.body:
Zero hydrophobic contribution here means H = 0. Therefore aH − bH² = 0, so these terms drop out, leaving:

$${log}_{10}(\frac{1}{IC_{50}}) = 2cE + d$$

steps.heading: Step 2 — Express IC50 directly
steps.body:
Use the general logarithm rule:

$${log}_{A}(M) = N$$

This is equivalent to:

$${A}^{N} = M$$

Apply this rule with base 10:

$$\frac{1}{IC_{50}} = {10}^{2cE + d}$$

Taking the reciprocal gives:

$$IC_{50} = \frac{1}{{10}^{2cE + d}}$$

steps.heading: Step 3 — Follow what happens as E changes
steps.body:
c and d are fixed numbers; E is the variable. Because c > 0, increasing E increases the exponent 2cE + d. The denominator therefore becomes larger, so IC₅₀ becomes smaller.

For very large positive E, the denominator is very large. Dividing 1 by that large number gives a value close to zero. Thus IC₅₀ decreases towards zero as E increases. Conversely, decreasing E makes the exponent and denominator smaller. When we divide 1 by a very small positive number, the resulting IC₅₀ is larger.

At E = 0 (the y-intercept of the graph), the value is as below:

$$IC_{50} = \frac{1}{{10}^{d}}$$

This is a positive number and hence the y intercept is a positive number along the y-axis.

A power of 10 is always positive, even when the exponent is negative. For example, if the exponent 2cE + d is −1:

$${10}^{-1} = 0.1$$

$$IC_{50} = \frac{1}{0.1}$$

$$IC_{50} = 10$$

If the exponent is +1 instead:

$${10}^{1} = 10$$

$$IC_{50} = \frac{1}{10}$$

$$IC_{50} = 0.1$$

Both examples give positive IC₅₀ values at E=0. Hence the y intercept is a positive number along the y-axis.

steps.heading: Step 4 — Select the graph
steps.body: Graph B decreases smoothly and flattens towards zero, matching the equation. Therefore the answer is B.

steps.heading: Shortcut
steps.body: Increasing E makes 10²ᶜᴱ⁺ᵈ larger. Its reciprocal becomes smaller and approaches zero. Choose the decreasing curve that flattens towards zero: B.

eliminations.reason: A increases as E increases, reversing the predicted direction. C turns upwards after decreasing, and D turns downwards after increasing. With c > 0 and d constant, the exponent increases throughout, so neither turning behaviour is possible.
